claims.claim: T-26271's CI diff failures ('recently enabled the sync impersonation flag', dry-run apply forbidden for argocd-server) are the direct consequence of RFC-001's impersonation design: once application.sync.impersonation.enabled is on, operations run as the AppProject's defaultServiceAccount rather than the broad cluster credential, so a server-side diff dry-run fails when that service account lacks the RBAC being granted. The reporter is chasing the cluster Secret; the identity actually acting is the impersonated one.

T-28695 and T-26271 report the same error string from two components of the same design gap: RFC-001 wires destinationServiceAccounts impersonation into the sync path only, so the Server-Side Diff path still acts as the standing cluster-Secret credential (application-controller on external clusters in T-28695, argocd-server for the CLI diff in T-26271). RFC-001's Security Considerations section is left as unanswered template questions, so the diff-identity split is unacknowledged in the design.

The strategy document commits that 'Deletion of generated Applications is explicitly out of scope for rollout orchestration: ordered or automated deletion of ApplicationSet children will not be implemented,' while the PRD proposes exactly that: a deletionOrder field (AllAtOnce/Reverse) in ApplicationSetStrategy implementing ordered, automated deletion of ApplicationSet children. Both commitments cannot hold; note-2 raised the disagreement and left it undecided.

RFC-001's stated goal is 'The feature can be enabled/disabled only at the system level. Once enabled/disabled, it is applicable to all Argo CD Applications,' but the platform sync decided impersonation rollout 'goes behind a per-project flag, not fleet-wide,' and T-26271's field report already describes flipping the flag per project. The rollout decision and the field deployment contradict the approved design's enablement model.

The PRD's Reverse deletionOrder 'waits for one application to be fully deleted before moving onto the next' and declares 'No immediate Risks to consider,' but T-28511 shows the failure mode already in the field: with rollingSync plus reverse deletion, an Application stuck Progressing means the deletion wait never completes and the applicationset-controller loops the app between Deleting and Syncing. Shipping the PRD without addressing this bakes a known infinite-loop mechanism into the new strategy.

T-24578's request for DAG-based Application destroy ordering across ApplicationSets and the PRD's deletionOrder proposal describe the same underlying need (controlled teardown of ApplicationSet-generated Applications) without citing each other; the PRD's Reverse strategy only covers a single ApplicationSet's rollingSync order, which does not satisfy T-24578's cross-ApplicationSet case.

T-26443's symptom (auto-sync applying very old manifests when the syncSource changes, observed only in push-to-stage mode) is explained by RFC-002's push-to-stage design decision: 'Argo CD relies on some external system to move changes to the deployment branch,' so nothing in Argo CD guarantees freshness of what the stage branch holds when auto-sync fires.

RFC-002's push-to-stage mode is the designated 'integration point for automated environment promotion systems,' and T-26443 shows syncing depends on that promoter moving fresh manifests; note-1 records that 'our stage-branch promoter is still the shell script, nobody owns it' and parks the question. A load-bearing, unowned shell script sits between hydration and deployment for every push-to-stage application.

RFC-002's founding opinion is that 'every change to an application's desired state must originate from a commit to a single GitOps repository' flowing dry-to-hydrated through the promotion path, while T-27327 proposes that rollback 'directly updates the sync branch (bypassing the staging branch)' via checkout of old rendered manifests with no corresponding dry commit. A rollback commit under that proposal is a deployed change with no dry-commit lineage, breaking the rule RFC-002 says promotion systems rely on ('prod may never be more than one dry hash ahead of test').

T-27949's pilot combines the source hydrator with RollingSync, and the incident review confirmed each hydrator push restarts the rolling sync wave; RFC-002 guarantees exactly this cadence (every dry commit produces a hydrated commit to the syncSource branch the children deploy from). Additionally T-27875 shows that a new commit arriving while a sync is in progress can leave apps OutOfSync indefinitely via the Status.Sync.Revision comparison bug — hydrated branches, with their frequent machine-generated commits, are the workload most likely to hit that window.

T-28927 aims to promote Progressive Sync to Stable, but the observability requested in T-27846 (metrics for wave start, step duration, refresh attribution, 'why is my sync waiting') is still an open proposal, and T-27949's own logs section shows the failure was invisible ('logs were at warn level, so no relevant progressive-sync transition logs were emitted'). Promoting to Stable before T-27846 lands means the feature's known failure modes (wave restarts, silent OutOfSync completion) remain unmeasurable in production.

T-27949 shows RollingSync reporting a rollout complete while child Applications are OutOfSync (specChanged lost, syncDesiredApplications only syncs Pending), directly against T-28927's Stable bar that features be 'tested and validated with various use cases' and mature; the Stable promotion issue does not list this correctness bug among its remaining scope.

T-27833's proposal (namespace bootstrapping by the Argo CD control-plane SA, sync by an impersonated SA stripped of kind: Namespace permissions) is an extension of RFC-001's impersonation model that RFC-001 does not anticipate: RFC-001 determines the service account per Application, not per resource kind, so the split T-27833 needs to close its clusterResourceWhitelist escape has no home in the approved design.

T-24417's gap (DrySource cannot point at a chart in a Helm repository, forcing helm dependencies) follows from two deliberate RFC-002 decisions: drySource carries only repoURL, targetRevision, and path, and external Helm values/charts are handled by recommending 'the umbrella chart approach' rather than multi-source. The ticket is field evidence of the cost RFC-002 accepted ('simplification is worth the cost of convenience').

RFC-002 introduces a repository-write credential (secret-type: repository-write) for a component that pushes machine-generated commits whose README/metadata attribute the dry commit's human author, and T-28239 records that those pushed commits are unsigned — so if signature verification is enforced on the hydrated branch, Argo CD rejects its own output, and until signing lands nothing distinguishes a legitimate hydrator push from any other holder of the write credential. Authorship of the system-of-record branch cannot currently be proven.

Compliance exposure of the impersonation rollout: RFC-001 answers that Kubernetes audit trails capture both the actual and impersonated user, but T-28695 shows the diff path still acts as the standing cluster credential ('User "argocd" cannot patch'), and its RBAC workaround history (five rounds of widening patch grants on a least-privilege role) means the old broad identity is being progressively re-widened to serve reads while review attention has moved to the new impersonated identities. The audit and review processes follow the new identity; the widening happens on the old one.

T-9095 (respect users' existing K8s RBAC for UI actions instead of duplicating it in Argo CD) and RFC-001 (respect tenants' existing K8s RBAC for sync instead of duplicating it in AppProjects) converge on the same access model — Kubernetes-native RBAC as the single source of authorization — from the UI and controller sides respectively, without referencing each other; RFC-001's deferred 'support to impersonate users or groups can be added in future' is the mechanism T-9095 would need.

proposals.change: Record the root cause on the ticket: with sync impersonation enabled, the diff runs as the destination service account, which lacks patch on cluster-scoped resources; the cluster Secret credential is not the acting identity and is a dead end for the reporter.
proposals.citedLine: the CI diff failures (the missing-permissions one, T-26271) got root-caused on the call: with impersonation on, diff runs as the destination service account which doesn't hold patch on cluster-scoped stuff. someone should note the root cause on that ticket so the reporter stops chasing the cluster secret.

proposals.change: Record that the hydrator History & Rollback work is deprioritized to next quarter and the dev pair has moved to the progressive sync deletion work.
proposals.citedLine: hydrator rollback work (the history & rollback ticket, T-27327) is deprioritized to next quarter. dev pair moves to the progressive sync deletion loop instead. ticket should say so.

proposals.change: Record that the delete/recreate loop reproduced in staging with the reverse deletion order, and record the interim runbook mitigation: switch the ApplicationSet to AllAtOnce deletion before manually deleting any child app, until the controller fix lands.
proposals.citedLine: the delete/recreate loop (T-28511) reproduced in staging with the reverse deletion order. mitigation for now: incident runbook says switch the ApplicationSet to AllAtOnce deletion before deleting any child app by hand. that's the operational rule until the controller fix lands — worth remembering as a standing practice.

proposals.change: Record the confirmed interaction (each hydrator push restarts the rolling sync wave) and the interim restriction from the incident review: hydrator pilot repos must not use progressive sync until a debounce exists.
proposals.citedLine: the wave-restart thing on hydrated repos: we confirmed each hydrator push restarts the rolling sync wave. interim call from the review: hydrator pilot repos must not use progressive sync until there's a debounce. the pilot ticket (T-27949) should carry that restriction so the next team doesn't trip it.

deltas.body: Impersonation rollout is gated behind a per-project flag, not fleet-wide, and no project enables it until the diff identity problem is fixed.
deltas.citedLine: impersonation rollout: we decided it goes behind a per-project flag, not fleet-wide. nobody flips it on a project until the diff story is fixed. that's a real decision, not a maybe.

deltas.body: Hydrator History & Rollback work is deprioritized to next quarter; the dev pair is reassigned to the progressive sync deletion work.
deltas.citedLine: hydrator rollback work (the history & rollback ticket, T-27327) is deprioritized to next quarter. dev pair moves to the progressive sync deletion loop instead. ticket should say so.

deltas.body: Standing operational rule until the controller fix lands: before manually deleting any child app of a progressive-sync ApplicationSet, switch the ApplicationSet to AllAtOnce deletion.
deltas.citedLine: the delete/recreate loop (T-28511) reproduced in staging with the reverse deletion order. mitigation for now: incident runbook says switch the ApplicationSet to AllAtOnce deletion before deleting any child app by hand. that's the operational rule until the controller fix lands — worth remembering as a standing practice.

deltas.body: Interim rule from the incident review: hydrator pilot repos must not use progressive sync until a debounce for hydrator-push wave restarts exists.
deltas.citedLine: the wave-restart thing on hydrated repos: we confirmed each hydrator push restarts the rolling sync wave. interim call from the review: hydrator pilot repos must not use progressive sync until there's a debounce. the pilot ticket (T-27949) should carry that restriction so the next team doesn't trip it.
